_about: The rejection floor: every creative decline Krish has made, in his exact words, with the rule it set and the check that now enforces it. Nothing is briefed, generated, carded to Codex or shown to Krish without first reading `python3 growth.py floor --format <format>` and checking the finished file against it. The same pattern as content-engine's rejection floor (scripts/floor.py). A new decline is added here in the same session it happens, with his words verbatim; a paraphrase stays an observation. Collected on 2026-11-09 from CHANGES.md, docs/briefs/2026-11-02-funny-bar.md, factory/bank/lines.json, heartside codex cards and the claude/runway-motion-batch records.

Dramatic light streaks read as painted on; ordinary daylight reads as real. Answer Krish's realism question dog by dog, honestly.

entries.made: Day 1 of the 16 to 22 Nov sprint, after the pristine alibi films
words: I want to nail down how: are we going for obviously AI, or are we going for photorealistic? I want this to feel like dogs making decisions or doing things that humans would do, for example, the parody LinkedIn 'wake up at 4am' inspiration post. If we're going for AI-generated visuals, then it should be comically exaggerated and absurd. Whereas if we're going for photorealism, then it should be dogs behaving like normal dogs, but then the text overlays, the captions, or something else humanizes the dog's behavior. Either way, the motif is always that the dog has a personality and is thinking about stuff in ways you forget as a viewer sometimes.
i recommend a blend of the above styles, but never a blurring
Yes, fully human acts
entries.rule: Every piece commits to one register and never mixes them. Photoreal: a scruffy real pet on the owner's phone doing only what a real dog does; the words (labels, caption, the note) supply the human thinking. Absurd: unmistakably staged, comically exaggerated dogs living a human format (the 4am LinkedIn routine); no attempt to pass as real footage. A near-real dog doing a slightly human thing is the blur and fails. Both registers carry the same motif: the dog has a personality and is thinking about things the viewer forgets it can. The sentiment lane is always photoreal. The product end card is the store's real render in both. In the absurd register the dog may do the human act itself: type at a desk, hold the coffee, stand at the podium, on its hind legs if the scene needs it (Krish, 17 Nov). The photoreal register keeps every real-dog limit.
entries.check: review: name the piece's register in its brief; tier 1 asks one-register on every contact sheet

entries.rule: A queued message reaches Codex only when its current turn ends, and Claude cannot put a message into a running turn; only Krish's Send now in Codex Desktop can. So every studio order ends its turn at a natural review point (at most one set, about 6 jobs) and closes with "Then end the turn and tell me in one line"; no order says not to stop or not to pause.
